stories.headline: Avalanche open season with 8-4 rout of Kings; MacKinnon scores twice, adds rare fight
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche began their 2026-27 season on a high note Wednesday night, defeating the Los Angeles Kings 8-4 in their home opener. Nathan MacKinnon was the standout performer, scoring twice during a dominant four-goal second period and capping his night with a rare fight.

The victory gave Colorado an early statement win to start the new campaign. MacKinnon's willingness to drop the gloves added an unexpected physical edge to an already impressive offensive performance.

The Avalanche had released their final roster cuts ahead of the opener and entered the game with a largely settled lineup. The convincing win over a Kings squad that has been a consistent playoff contender in recent seasons will be welcomed by fans eager for a championship run.

stories.headline: Nuggets sign Ryan Nembhard to two-way contract, waive CU fan favorite KJ Simpson
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets have agreed to a two-way contract with guard Ryan Nembhard, 23, after he cleared waivers following a trade from Dallas to Charlotte and a subsequent waiver by the Hornets, a league source told The Denver Post on Wednesday. To make room, the team will waive KJ Simpson, the former CU Buffalo who signed a two-way deal with Denver in February.

Nembhard played 60 games as a rookie for Dallas last season and torched the Nuggets for 28 points and 10 assists in December. He posted a 3.72 assist-to-turnover ratio and shot 41.5% from the field, making him viewed as an upgrade to Denver's point guard depth behind Jamal Murray.

Simpson, 24, appeared in just six games for Denver after signing his two-way contract. His release comes at an awkward moment, as the Nuggets are holding training camp in Boulder this week and are scheduled to play a preseason game at CU on Sunday. It remains unclear whether Simpson will stay with the G League affiliate Grand Rapids Gold or seek a new opportunity.

stories.headline: Denver man sentenced to 40 years in prison for fatally shooting his wife
stories.summary:
Tyler Nelson, 32, was sentenced Wednesday to 40 years in prison for the second-degree murder of his wife, Breanna Canter, 30, Denver District Judge Stephanie Scoville ruled. A jury convicted Nelson in August after he shot and killed Canter at their apartment in Denver's Windsor neighborhood in September 2024, with their young son asleep in the next room.

Nelson called 911 in the early morning hours of Sept. 24, 2024, claiming he had accidentally shot Canter during a drunken argument about gun safety. Investigators found inconsistencies between his account, the physical evidence at the crime scene, and Canter's injuries, leading to his arrest and charges of first-degree murder and first-degree assault.

"Breanna Canter was a loving mother and beloved daughter whose murder was a terrible tragedy, most profoundly for her young son and her parents," Denver District Attorney John Walsh said in a statement. "Today's sentence ensures that Tyler Nelson pays a heavy price for his despicable actions and provides a measure of justice for Breanna, her family, and her friends."

stories.headline: Nearly 6,000 legal immigrants in Colorado to lose Medicaid coverage under federal 'big, beautiful bill'
stories.summary:
An estimated 5,900 documented immigrants in Colorado will lose Medicaid coverage starting Thursday under provisions of H.R. 1, the federal legislation known as the "big, beautiful bill," the Colorado Department of Health Care Policy and Financing announced. The cuts affect refugees, asylum recipients, Afghan humanitarian parolees who aided U.S. military operations, Native Americans born in Canada, and victims of domestic violence or human trafficking who were granted legal status.

Green card holders, people from Pacific island nations under the Compact of Free Association, and certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants will retain eligibility, as will legally present children and pregnant or postpartum adults in otherwise ineligible categories. The Colorado department initially estimated about 5,000 people would lose coverage before revising the figure upward Wednesday.

Clinicians at the University of Colorado's Anschutz Medical Campus, where most patients in the immigrant and refugee mental health program rely on Medicaid, said staff are scrambling to determine continued eligibility and connect patients with free or low-cost community providers. The Congressional Budget Office estimates the national cuts will leave approximately 100,000 people without insurance and save $6.2 billion over 10 years, while the broader Medicaid changes in the bill are projected to remove coverage from more than 7 million Americans.

stories.headline: Rep. Gabe Evans announces reelection bid for Colorado's competitive 8th Congressional District
stories.summary:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans has announced he is running for reelection to Colorado's 8th Congressional District, one of the most competitive swing districts in the state. Evans, a Republican, has pointed to crime rates and fentanyl deaths in the Denver metro area as central issues motivating his continued service.

The 8th Congressional District, which covers portions of the northern Denver metro and extends toward Greeley, has been a closely watched battleground since the district was created following the 2020 census. Evans flipped the seat from Democrat Yadira Caraveo in 2024.

His reelection announcement sets up what is expected to be another competitive general election contest in November. Democrats have flagged the district as a top pickup opportunity as they seek to reclaim the House majority.

stories.headline: Update: Southern Colorado faces life-threatening flooding as triple storm system moves through; Denver totals lower than feared
stories.summary:
A converging "triple-threat" storm system continued to bring heavy rainfall to southern Colorado through Thursday morning, with AccuWeather warning of "life-threatening flooding" possible south of Colorado 94, roughly in line with Colorado Springs. Some areas south of the Palmer Divide could see 4 to 8 inches of rain, forecasters said, with flood watches in effect for 13 counties including Pueblo, El Paso, Las Animas and Baca.

The storm draws moisture from the remnants of Hurricane Polo and Tropical Storm Odalys, which are merging with an existing trough bringing cold air and rain, AccuWeather said. The setup is similar to last fall's Tropical Storms Priscilla and Raymond, which flooded more than 100 homes in La Plata County alone.

Denver's forecast improved significantly Wednesday morning, with the National Weather Service dropping expected totals for the metro from nearly 1.5 inches to roughly a quarter inch. The heaviest accumulations near Denver are expected along and south of the Palmer Divide, where 1 to 2.5 inches may fall. The storm is expected to clear the region by midday Thursday, with a warm and sunny weekend to follow.

stories.headline: Update: Denver Water lawn-watering ban takes effect Oct. 1; violators face fines up to $1,000
stories.summary:
Denver Water's ban on lawn watering and spray irrigation officially took effect Thursday, with the utility warning customers that violations will carry steep financial penalties. Residential customers caught watering their lawns face a $500 fine for a first offense, rising to $1,000 for each subsequent violation, with service shutoff possible for persistent violators.

The utility, which serves 1.5 million people across the metro area, has sent postcards to customers serving as formal warnings. Multifamily and nonresidential customers face higher fines — $1,000 for a first offense and $2,000 plus service suspension for repeat violations. Hand-watering of trees, shrubs, flowers and vegetables is still permitted under the ban.

Denver Water's reservoirs stood at just 67% of capacity as of this week, compared with a typical 91% at the start of fall. Officials said the ban could save 5,000 acre-feet of water — enough to serve more than 10,000 families for a year — and cautioned that even a strong winter snowpack is unlikely to fully replenish storage levels.

stories.headline: Amazon's Zoox robotaxis coming to Denver streets this winter for snow and ice testing
stories.summary:
Amazon's autonomous vehicle subsidiary Zoox will deploy a small test fleet of robotaxis in Denver for several months this winter, the company confirmed to 9NEWS. The vehicles will not be available for public rides; instead, the fleet is designed to train Zoox's driving technology on winter conditions including heavy rain, snow and ice — conditions largely unavailable at the company's California testing grounds.

Zoox joins a growing list of autonomous vehicle companies eyeing Denver as a testing environment for challenging weather scenarios. The city's combination of urban street grids and unpredictable winter weather makes it an attractive proving ground for self-driving systems.

No specific start date or the number of vehicles to be deployed was disclosed. Residents can expect to see the distinctively designed, bidirectional Zoox vehicles — which have no steering wheel and face both directions — navigating Denver streets in the coming months.

stories.headline: Denver vision AI firm ROC wins $64.3 million Justice Department contract for digital evidence software
stories.summary:
ROC, a Denver-based computer vision company, has been awarded a $64.3 million contract by the U.S. Department of Justice to build digital evidence software for use in criminal prosecutions, the Denver Business Journal reported. The contract represents one of the largest federal awards secured by a Colorado technology firm this year.

ROC specializes in artificial intelligence tools for analyzing visual data, and its new software will be used to manage and process digital evidence across federal prosecutions. The company has been growing its footprint in the law enforcement and public safety technology sector.

The contract is a significant milestone for Denver's technology industry, underscoring the city's emergence as a hub for AI and computer vision companies competing for high-value government work.

stories.headline: Denver International Airport explores childcare for 43,000 workers amid Colorado's persistent child care shortage
stories.summary:
Denver International Airport, one of Colorado's largest employers, is opening a 20-spot drop-in childcare center at its new training facility early next year and is researching the cost and feasibility of providing care for all 43,000 of its employees. A survey of airport workers found more than half of parents with young children had considered leaving their jobs or cutting hours due to childcare challenges, with 84% reporting they rearrange work schedules because of care issues.

The initiative reflects a broader shift among Colorado employers who increasingly view childcare as a workforce issue rather than a private family matter. A 2024 survey found that 32% of Colorado parents had quit a job due to childcare problems, and another 20% reported being let go or fired as a result.

The new childcare center will serve participants in the airport's Center of Equity and Excellence in Aviation training program, which aims to build talent pipelines for the aviation industry. Airport officials said childcare access was identified early as a barrier to participation in the program. The Boulder Chamber of Commerce and other business groups across the region have also amplified calls for employer-supported childcare solutions as vacancies persist across multiple industries.

stories.headline: Mountain pine beetle infestation expands dramatically across Colorado's Front Range ponderosa forests
stories.summary:
A mountain pine beetle outbreak is spreading rapidly through Colorado's ponderosa pine forests, with impacted acreage increasing 148% to 5,544 acres in 2025 compared to 2024, according to the Colorado State Forest Service. Entomologist Dan West warned that activity in 2026 is expected to be two to three times greater than last year, putting more than 600,000 acres of ponderosa forest and the roughly 4 million people living among them at elevated risk.

Historic drought has weakened the trees' natural defenses, allowing beetles to kill pines throughout foothill communities stretching from Boulder to Colorado Springs and beyond. On some mountain properties about 40 miles west of Denver, nearly every pine is dead, and removal costs — which can run $15,000 per acre — are out of reach for many residents.

A U.S. Forest Service projection map shows dark red infestation zones blanketing forests at every latitude along the Front Range through 2030. Beyond aesthetic and property damage, the die-off heightens wildfire risk and threatens the watersheds that supply drinking water to millions of metro-area residents. A century of fire suppression combined with climate-driven drought and heat are cited as primary contributors to the crisis.

stories.headline: New Denver restaurant Blossom by SYC brings elevated Peking duck experience to the city
stories.summary:
Restaurateur Shuang "Sherry" Crossland has opened Blossom by SYC at 1691 Central St. in Denver, aiming to establish what she describes as the city's first elevated Chinese dining concept. The space features jade, pink and gold decor with faux floral ceilings designed to evoke a "girls' night out" atmosphere, and is led by executive chef Adam Chan, a Hong Kong native who previously worked at the two-Michelin-starred TATE Dining Room in Hong Kong.

The restaurant's centerpiece is a tableside Peking duck experience, with ducks roasted in a custom German-imported oven and carved in front of diners. The menu also includes pork soup dumplings, black truffle pork shao mai, wagyu chow fun and lychee shrimp balls stuffed with mozzarella, alongside larger entrees such as miso black cod and braised beef short rib.

Crossland, founder of One Concept Restaurant Group and SYC Concepts, researched the concept through dining trips to New York, Las Vegas, Miami and China, including a visit to a prominent Beijing duck restaurant. Blossom represents her latest expansion of a metro Denver restaurant portfolio that began with Go Fish in 2007. Happy hour and weekend brunch offerings are planned for future phases.

topStory.headline: GOP Candidates Weigh Trump's Electoral Value Against Voter Skepticism Ahead of Midterms
topStory.summary:
As the 2026 midterm elections approach, Republicans face a strategic tension over former President Donald Trump's role in motivating the party's base voters. While Trump remains a powerful draw for core Republican supporters, some candidates in competitive districts are reluctant to align too closely with him, reflecting concerns about his standing with broader electorates.

A central flashpoint is voter skepticism toward Trump's economic promises. A recent YouGov poll of 6,051 American adults found that only 20 percent said they believed they would receive the $5,000 payment Trump has pledged if Republicans retain control of Congress, while 64 percent said they definitely or probably would not receive it. The finding suggests that even some Trump supporters are treating his economic pledges with caution rather than confidence.

The divide extends to how media outlets are framing Trump's economic agenda. The Washington Post described his consumer-focused efforts as 'ideas' facing external resistance, while the progressive outlet MS NOW characterized them as 'gimmicks' that are losing traction with voters. Analysts noted the Post's language as a sign of a stated effort toward more balanced news coverage under owner Jeff Bezos.

Voter sentiment within the Republican base itself is showing signs of nuance. Missouri Republican Jeremy Cove, 44, told the Associated Press that while he voted for Trump and supports him broadly, some administration actions have eroded his trust. Commentators including Mike Cernovich have pointed to what economists call a K-shaped recovery, in which asset holders are prospering while wage earners continue to struggle, as a source of persistent economic discontent that political messaging has not resolved.

The dynamic puts Republican candidates in a difficult position heading into campaign season. Alienating Trump risks suppressing base turnout, but close association with unpopular economic outcomes or unfulfilled promises could cost votes in swing districts. How individual candidates navigate that balance is expected to be a defining feature of the 2026 midterm landscape.
